      <content name="title">Depression</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Dysthymic <span class="qt1">Disorder</span></content>
      <content name="altTitle">Clinical depression</content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt3">Major</span> <span class="qt0">depressive</span> <span class="qt1">disorder</span></content>
      <content name="altTitle">Unipolar depression</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is depression?<p>Depression is more than a feeling of being sad or irritable for a few days. It's a serious mood <span class="qt1">disorder</span>. As one of the most common mental <span class="qt1">disorders</span> in the United States, depression can affect how you think, feel, and your everyday life. You may not know why you feel this way, but even basic daily activities such as sleeping, eating, or working may become difficult. Depression often needs long-term treatment but getting help at the earliest sign of a problem can help manage your symptoms.</p>What are the different types of depression?<p>The most common types of depression are <span class="qt3">major</span> depression and persistent <span class="qt0">depressive</span> <span class="qt1">disorder</span>.</p><ul><li><span class="qt3">Major</span> depression symptoms include a depressed mood or a loss of interest. Symptoms affect your daily activities and last for at least two weeks.</li><li>Persistent <span class="qt0">depressive</span> <span class="qt1">disorder</span> (also called dysthymia or dysthymic <span class="qt1">disorder</span>) has less severe <span class="qt0">depressive</span> symptoms, but they last longer, usually for at least two years.</li></ul><p>Other types of depression can include:</p><ul><li>Seasonal affective <span class="qt1">disorder</span> comes and goes with the seasons. It usually starts in late fall and early winter and goes away during the spring and summer.</li><li>Bipolar <span class="qt1">disorder</span> is sometimes called manic depression. This mood <span class="qt1">disorder</span> can cause intense mood swings.</li><li>Depression with symptoms of psychosis is a severe form of depression that also has delusions (false beliefs) or hallucinations (seeing, hearing, or feeling something that isn't there).</li></ul>What causes depression?<p>There are a variety of things that may cause depression, including genetic, biological, environmental, and psychological factors. Depression can happen at any age and can affect anyone, but it's more common in women. This is often due to the physical and hormonal changes that women have during menstruation, pregnancy, the postpartum period, and menopause. Other mental <span class="qt1">disorders</span> or chronic medical conditions such as diabetes, cancer, or heart <span class="qt2">disease</span> may occur with depression. This may make the chronic condition or depression worse.</p><p>In some cases, there is no clear cause for depression.</p>Who is at risk of depression?<p>You may be at a higher risk of depression if you have a close relative who has it or another mental health <span class="qt1">disorder</span>. Going through trauma or stressful life events may raise your risk even more.</p>What are the symptoms of depression?<p>Depression doesn't look the same on everyone. The type and number of symptoms of depression can vary and don't always appear like sadness. Depression may affect you differently based on your:</p><ul><li>Age. The symptoms of depression may be different in a child, who may appear more irritable than sad. Teens may act out or have excessive sleepiness. The symptoms for an older adult may not be as obvious as other age groups.</li><li>Sex. Men often show symptoms and coping behaviors differently than women. Rather than sad, men may appear angry or irritable.</li><li>Medical conditions. Some medicines and medical conditions may cause symptoms that look like depression. Chronic conditions may make depression worse.</li></ul><p>Symptoms of depression are ongoing and affect your day-to-day life. They can include:</p><ul><li>Feeling sad or "empty"</li><li>Losing interest in favorite activities</li><li>Overeating, or not wanting to eat at all</li><li>Sleeping too much, or not enough</li><li>Feeling very tired</li><li>Feeling hopeless, irritable, anxious, or guilty</li><li>Having aches and pains, headaches, cramps, or digestive problems</li><li>Having thoughts of death or suicide</li><li>Changing moods or behaviors</li><li>Increasing use of alcohol or drugs</li><li>Isolating from family and friends</li></ul>How is depression diagnosed?<p>If you think you have depression, talk to your health care provider or a mental health provider. To be diagnosed with depression, your provider may use many tools:</p><ul><li>A medical history will include asking about your symptoms and family history. To be diagnosed with depression, your symptoms must occur most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks. One of the symptoms must be a depressed mood or a loss of interest in most activities.</li><li>Medical tests may be done to rule out other medical conditions. Certain medicines and medical conditions (such as viruses or thyroid <span class="qt1">disorders</span>) may cause symptoms like depression.</li><li>A physical exam to make sure another issue isn't causing your symptoms.</li><li>A mental health evaluation by your provider or a mental health provider.</li></ul>What are the treatments for depression?<p>Depression may need long-term treatment. Most treatments include medicines and/or psychotherapy (talk therapy):</p><ul><li>Medicines such as antidepressants may help control your symptoms. You may need to try several medicines to find which works best for you. Medicine may take time to work and can have side effects. Don't stop taking your medicine without first talking with your provider. Contact your provider if you have any concerns about side effects from the medicine.</li><li>Psychotherapy (talk therapy) under the care of a mental health provider can help you recognize and change troubling emotions, thoughts, and behaviors. This may be done one-on-one or in a group setting. It can give you and your family support, education, skills, and coping strategies.</li><li>Light therapy has been shown to be effective for seasonal affective <span class="qt1">disorder</span> (SAD).</li><li>Other treatments options may be considered if treatment isn't working or if depression is severe. These may include:
	<ul><li>Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) is a brain stimulation procedure that uses a mild electric current when you are under general anesthesia. ECT is most often used for severe depression that is not getting better with other treatments.</li><li>Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) is a brain stimulation procedure that uses magnetic waves to relieve depression. It's not as powerful as ECT, but with rTMS, you don't need anesthesia. It also has a low risk of negative effects on your memory and thinking.</li></ul>
</li></ul>Can depression be prevented?<p>Most cases of depression can't be prevented, but healthy lifestyle changes can have long-term benefits for your mental health. These can include:</p><ul><li>Getting regular exercise</li><li>Having a consistent sleep schedule</li><li>Controlling stress</li></ul><p>If you, or someone you love is depressed, see your provider or a mental health provider. It's important to get treatment at the earliest sign of a problem.</p><p>If you or someone you know has thoughts of hurting themselves or attempting suicide, get help right away. If it is an emergency, dial 911.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Mental Health</p></content>

      <content name="title">Seasonal Affective <span class="qt1">Disorder</span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">SAD</content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt3">Major</span> <span class="qt0">depressive</span> <span class="qt1">disorder</span> with seasonal pattern</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Seasonal depression</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Seasonal mood <span class="qt1">disorder</span></content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Seasonal affective <span class="qt1">disorder</span> (SAD) is a type of depression that comes and goes with the seasons. It usually starts in the late fall and early winter and goes away during the spring and summer. Some people do have episodes of depression that start in the spring or summer, but that is a lot less common. Symptoms of SAD may include:</p><ul><li>Sadness</li><li>Gloomy outlook</li><li>Feeling hopeless, worthless, and irritable</li><li>Loss of interest or pleasure in activities you used to enjoy</li><li>Low energy</li><li>Difficulty sleeping or oversleeping</li><li>Carbohydrate cravings and weight gain</li><li>Thoughts of death or suicide</li></ul><p>SAD is more common in women, young people, and those who live far from the equator. You are also more likely to have SAD if you or your family members have depression.</p><p>The exact causes of SAD are unknown. Researchers have found that people with SAD may have an imbalance of serotonin, a brain chemical that affects your mood. Their bodies also make too much melatonin, a hormone that regulates sleep, and not enough vitamin D.</p><p>The main treatment for SAD is light therapy. The idea behind light therapy is to replace the sunshine that you miss during the fall and winter months. You sit in front of a light therapy box every morning to get daily exposure to bright, artificial light. But some people with SAD do not respond to light therapy alone. Antidepressant medicines and talk therapy can reduce SAD symptoms, either alone or combined with light therapy.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Mental Health</p></content>

    <document rank="2" url="https://medlineplus.gov/teendepression.html">
      <content name="title">Teen Depression</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Depression, Teen</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is depression in teens?<p>Depression in teens (ages 13-17) is a serious medical <span class="qt2">illness</span>. It's more than just a feeling of being sad or "blue" for a few days. It is an intense feeling of sadness, hopelessness, and anger or frustration that lasts much longer. These feelings make it hard for you to function normally and do your usual activities. You may also have trouble focusing and have no motivation or energy. Depression can make you feel like it is hard to enjoy life or even get through the day.</p>What causes depression in teens?<p>Many factors may play a role in depression, including:</p><ul><li>Genetics. Depression can run in families.</li><li>Brain biology and chemistry.</li><li>Hormones. Hormone changes can contribute to depression.</li><li>Stressful childhood events such as trauma, the death of a loved one, bullying, and abuse.</li></ul>Which teens are at risk of depression?<p>Depression can happen at any age, but often begins in the teens or early adulthood. Certain teens are at higher risk of depression, such as those who:</p><ul><li>Have other mental health conditions, such as anxiety, eating <span class="qt1">disorders</span>, and substance use</li><li>Have other <span class="qt2">diseases</span>, such as diabetes, cancer, and heart <span class="qt2">disease</span></li><li>Have family members with <span class="qt2">mental illness</span></li><li>Have a dysfunctional family/family conflict</li><li>Have problems with friends or other kids at school</li><li>Have learning disabilities or attention deficit hyperactivity <span class="qt1">disorder (ADHD</span>)</li><li>Have had trauma in childhood</li><li>Have low self-esteem, a pessimistic outlook, or poor coping skills</li></ul>What are the symptoms of depression in teens?<p>If you have depression, you have one or more of these symptoms most of the time:</p><ul><li>Sadness</li><li>Feeling of emptiness</li><li>Hopelessness</li><li>Being angry, irritable, or frustrated, even at minor things</li></ul><p>You also may also have other symptoms, such as:</p><ul><li>No longer caring about things you used to enjoy</li><li>Changes in weight, such as losing weight when you are not dieting or gaining weight from eating too much</li><li>Changes in sleep, such as having trouble falling asleep or staying asleep, or sleeping much more than usual</li><li>Feeling restless or having trouble sitting still</li><li>Feeling very tired or not having energy</li><li>Feeling worthless or very guilty</li><li>Having trouble concentrating, remembering information, or making decisions</li><li>Thinking about dying or suicide</li></ul>How is depression in teens diagnosed?<p>If you think you might be depressed, tell someone that you trust, such as your:</p><ul><li>Parents or guardian</li><li>Teacher or counselor</li><li>Doctor</li></ul><p>The next step is to see your doctor for a checkup. Your doctor can first make sure that you do not have another health problem that is causing your depression. To do this, you may have a physical exam and lab tests.</p><p>If you don't have another health problem, you will get a psychological evaluation. Your doctor may do it, or you may be referred to a mental health professional to get one. You may be asked about things such as:</p><ul><li>Your thoughts and feelings</li><li>How you are doing at school</li><li>Any changes in your eating, sleeping, or energy level</li><li>Whether you are suicidal</li><li>Whether you use alcohol or drugs</li></ul>How is depression in teens treated?<p>Effective treatments for depression in teens include talk therapy, or a combination of talk therapy and medicines:</p><p>Talk therapy</p><p>Talk therapy, also called psychotherapy or counseling, can help you understand and manage your moods and feelings. It involves going to see a therapist, such as a psychiatrist, a psychologist, a social worker, or counselor. You can talk out your emotions to someone who understands and supports you. You can also learn how to stop thinking negatively and start to look at the positives in life. This will help you build confidence and feel better about yourself.</p><p>There are many different types of talk therapy. Certain types have been shown to help teens deal with depression, including:</p><ul><li>Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), which helps you to identify and change negative and unhelpful thoughts. It also helps you build coping skills and change behavioral patterns.</li><li>Interpersonal therapy (IPT), which focuses on improving your relationships. It helps you understand and work through troubled relationships that may contribute to your depression. IPT may help you change behaviors that are causing problems.  You also explore <span class="qt3">major</span> issues that may add to your depression, such as grief or life changes.</li></ul><p>Medicines</p><p>In some cases, your doctor will suggest medicines along with talk therapy. There are a few antidepressants that have been widely studied and proven to help teens. If you are taking medicine for depression, it is important to see your doctor regularly.</p><p>It is also important to know that it will take some time for you to get relief from antidepressants:</p><ul><li>It can take 3 to 4 weeks until an antidepressant takes effect</li><li>You may have to try more than one antidepressant to find one that works for you</li><li>It can also take some time to find the right dose of an antidepressant</li></ul><p>In some cases, teenagers may have an increase in suicidal thoughts or behavior when taking antidepressants. This risk is higher in the first few weeks after starting the medicine and when the dose is changed. Make sure to tell your parents or guardian if you start feeling worse or have thoughts of hurting yourself.</p><p>You should not stop taking the antidepressants on your own. You need to work with your doctor to slowly and safely decrease the dose before you stop.</p><p>Programs for severe depression</p><p>Some teens who have severe depression or are at risk of hurting themselves may need more intensive treatment. They may go into a psychiatric hospital or do a day program. Both offer counseling, group discussions, and activities with mental health professionals and other patients. Day programs may be full-day or half-day, and they often last for several weeks.</p></content>
